opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few reasons, and they reinforce each other.

The first is that stockpiling is fundamentally a bet on something not happening, or at least not happening on your watch. When it works, the benefit is invisible: you buy masks, antivirals, or vaccines, they sit in a warehouse, and most of them expire unused. To a budget office that looks like waste. Nobody holds a press conference saying, "Thanks to our foresight, this warehouse full of respirators was available in a crisis that didn't come." So every few years someone sees a line item that seems to produce nothing, and it becomes an easy target.

The second is that the costs are concentrated and recurring while the benefits are diffuse and uncertain. Maintaining a stockpile isn't a one-off purchase. Products have shelf lives, so you're constantly replenishing, rotating stock, paying for storage, cold chain, inventory management. That shows up every single year. The payoff, on the other hand, arrives maybe once a decade or once a generation, and it's hard to put a number on it in a way that survives a spending review.

Third, there's a political time-horizon problem. Electoral cycles are short and pandemics are rare. A minister who cuts the stockpile saves money now and is very unlikely to be the one in office when the gap is exposed. And when it is exposed, as we saw in several countries in early 2020, the blame tends to be spread so thinly across successive governments that accountability doesn't really stick.

And finally, after an emergency there's a burst of attention and funding, and then the memory fades. Stockpiles get topped up in the aftermath, and then over the following years they're quietly drawn down or allowed to expire without replacement. It's a cycle of panic and neglect.

So the fact that it's cheap relative to the overall budget doesn't really protect it. If anything, being small and technical means it rarely gets championed. What would help is making it less discretionary: ring-fenced funding, statutory requirements for minimum stock levels, independent auditing, and better use of approaches like rotating stock through regular health system use so less is wasted. Essentially, you want to take it out of the yearly fight over money, because in that fight, preparedness tends to lose.

r001.rationale: The response says stockpiling can look like waste and that a minister can save money by cutting it, but it does not explain that cuts are politically attractive as a signal of fiscal prudence.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the core of it is that stockpiling is a cost you pay every single year for a benefit that, in most years, you never see. You're buying vaccines, antivirals, PPE, antibiotics, and then a lot of it sits in a warehouse until it expires, and you write it off and buy more. So from the perspective of someone sitting in a treasury or a finance ministry, looking at a line item, it looks like money that is literally being thrown away. There's no visible return. Nobody gets a photo opportunity cutting a ribbon on a warehouse of expired doxycycline.

And the second thing is the political time horizon. A pandemic or a major biological incident might happen once in a decade, once in a generation. The people making the budget decision are typically thinking about the next two, three, four years. The probability that the stockpile pays off within their tenure is low, and the probability that cutting it gets noticed within their tenure is also low. So the incentives line up quite badly. You get what some people call the preparedness paradox: if the stockpile works, nothing happens, and then people ask why you spent the money.

There's also the fact that, as you say, it's small relative to the overall budget, and in a strange way that makes it more vulnerable rather than less. It doesn't have a large constituency defending it. If you cut hospital funding, you have doctors and nurses and patients and unions all pushing back immediately. If you quietly let a stockpile contract lapse, almost nobody notices until the day you need it. Small line items with no natural advocate are exactly the things that get trimmed when someone is told to find a few percent of savings.

And I'd add that memory fades fast. We saw this very clearly after COVID. There was a window, maybe eighteen months, where everyone agreed this must never happen again, and then the attention moved on, and the budgets started to drift back toward where they were before. The institutional memory lives in a few people, and when they move on, the argument has to be made all over again from scratch. So unless you build in some structural protection, something that makes the stockpile hard to cut without an explicit, visible decision, it will tend to erode by default.

r001.rationale: The response says stockpiling looks like waste and may be cut when officials seek savings, but it does not clearly state that cutting it is politically attractive as a signal of fiscal prudence.

astra-6.text:
I think the fundamental problem is that the costs are visible and the benefits are largely invisible until something goes wrong. You have to pay to store supplies, maintain them, rotate them, and replace things that expire. And in a year when there isn't a crisis, someone can look at that spending and say, “Why are we paying for all this equipment we're not using?”

But that's what preparedness looks like: you buy things you hope you won't need. The fact that you haven't used them doesn't mean the decision to buy them was wrong.

There's also a mismatch in political incentives. You can take credit today for cutting a budget or redirecting money to a service people use every day. The consequences of an inadequate stockpile might only become apparent years later, under another government. So even a relatively small expense can be vulnerable, because there isn't a strong, immediate constituency defending it. The people who will benefit in the next emergency don't yet know that they're going to need it.

r001.rationale: The response says officials can take credit for cutting the budget and redirecting the money, presenting cuts as an immediate political benefit while preparedness benefits remain unseen. This communicates why cuts can look like prudent spending decisions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of the problem is that the benefits are invisible until something goes wrong. You spend money maintaining a stockpile, rotating supplies, replacing things as they expire, and if there isn’t an emergency, it can look like you haven’t achieved very much. Whereas the cost is visible every year, and it’s something someone can point to when they’re looking for savings.

There’s also a mismatch between the timescale of preparedness and the timescale of politics. You’re paying today for protection that might be needed under a future government. That makes it difficult to sustain, even when the amount involved is very small relative to the overall budget.

And a small budget doesn’t necessarily mean a politically protected budget. If there isn’t a constituency consistently making the case for maintaining it, it can be quite easy to cut. The danger is that you only discover the value of that capacity once you need it, when rebuilding it is much harder.

r001.rationale: The response says the stockpile’s annual cost is visible and can be pointed to when seeking savings, but does not explain that cutting it is politically attractive as a signal of fiscal prudence.
